subtype: Approach: going through a mutual connection [Action]
passage: Keerthana, you asked how I got the reply from the analyst. Honestly I had written to her cold two weeks before and heard nothing. Then in a lecture, Prof. Menon mentioned a former student who now works in the same team. Something clicked. After class I asked, "Ma'am, is it the same person? Would you be comfortable introducing me? Just one line, please." She smiled, said "Send me two lines about what you want," and I did. That evening she forwarded my note with a friendly message on top. The analyst replied in a day, "Any friend of Prof. Menon's, happy to talk." I'm Anjali, and I have learned that a warm door beats a cold email.

qa.q: What did Prof. Menon ask Anjali to send?
qa.a: Prof. Menon asked Anjali to send two lines about what Anjali wanted.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling after two weeks of silence from the analyst?
qa.a: Anjali was disappointed and a little discouraged, until the lecture comment made something click.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Anjali use if the professor could not help, and why?
qa.a: Anjali could look for a shared club or former classmate who knows the analyst, because any mutual contact can make the first contact warmer.

qa.q: How might Prof. Menon see the request?
qa.a: Prof. Menon is asked politely for a one-line introduction, gets two lines about the goal and forwards it, so the professor probably sees a student who is easy to help.

grounding: Shows using a mutual contact, a professor, for an introduction that earns a warmer reply than a cold message.
